arXiv:2606.08158v1 [cs.CL] 06 Jun 2026

Constrained Paraphrase Consistency for LLM Hallucination Detection

Shanshan Lin    Dongsheng Hong    Sibo Ju    Chao Chen    Xi Zhang    Xiangwen Liao
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) can generate factually inconsistent claims, motivating accurate and scalable hallucination detectors. Prior work largely enlarges training sets via synthesis or new annotations, introducing increasing cost and potential bias while underusing the consistency implied by semantically equivalent paraphrases. We propose Consistency-Constrained Hallucination Detector (CCHD), which formulates training as a constrained optimization problem. The standard cross-entropy on original document-claim pairs is complemented by (i) paraphrase-consistency constraints bounding divergence across paraphrased views, and (ii) label-preservation constraints tying paraphrases to ground truth. We solve the problem by gradient descent-ascent over model parameters and per-view Lagrange multipliers, adding only a few scalar dual variables and no inference-time overhead. With DeBERTa and Flan-T5 backbones, CCHD consistently outperforms strong baselines (FactCG, MiniCheck, and AlignScore) on standard factuality benchmarks, demonstrating its superiority on hallucination detection.

Index Terms: 
Constrained optimization, hallucination detection, large language model

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent text for tasks such as abstractive summarization [15]. However, they are prone to factual hallucinations, where outputs appear grammatical but contain unsupported or incorrect information [13]. Prior work [7, 8] reports that up to 30% of generated summaries contain factual inconsistencies, motivating scalable methods to automatically detect factual consistency. Fig. 1 shows an example from the hallucination detection task.

Research on factuality detection follows two paradigms. One line prompts powerful LLMs to act as judges via sampling, self-consistency, or critique [12, 14, 19]. However, these evaluators are computationally expensive because they require multiple LLM calls per instance. Another line of studies train lightweight discriminative detectors on document-claim pairs, e.g., NLI-based SummaC [9], MiniCheck [17], and graph-augmented FactCG [10]. This line of work prioritizes data generation (via synthetic augmentation or new annotations) to expand coverage, incurring extra costs. Moreover, they (i) underexplore structure present in existing data that semantically equivalent paraphrases of a claim should yield consistent predictions for a fixed document; and (ii) often treat original and synthetic samples identically, despite potential bias and noise in these synthetic samples.

We address these limitations by introducing Consistency-Constrained Hallucination Detector (CCHD). Our premise is simple: if a document supports (or contradicts) a claim, any semantically equivalent paraphrase should receive the same prediction. CCHD formalizes this premise and casts training as a constrained optimization problem that enforces prediction-level agreements across multiple paraphrase views. Concretely, CCHD sets the standard cross-entropy on original examples as primary objective, while two families of soft constraints regulate paraphrased views: (i) paraphrase-consistency constraints that bound the divergence between the original prediction and its paraphrased counterparts; and (ii) label-preservation constraints that keep each paraphrase aligned with the ground-truth label, with controllable slack to accommodate potential noise in paraphrased text. CCHD solves the problem via gradient descent-ascent (GDA) over model parameters and per-view Lagrange multipliers [11, 4], adaptively balancing supervision and consistency without introducing inference-time overhead.

Empirically, CCHD outperforms strong baselines, including FactCG [10], MiniCheck [17], and Alignscore [20] across 11 factuality tasks in the LLM-AggreFact benchmark. Sensitivity analysis and ablation studies further confirm the importance of each component.

In summary, our contributions are as follows: (1) We cast hallucination detection as a constrained optimization problem that enforces prediction-level agreement across semantically equivalent paraphrases. (2) We propose CCHD, which instantiates paraphrase views by back-translation without extra annotation, and solves the constrained problem with GDA over per-view Lagrange multipliers, adding no inference-time overhead. (3) With Flan-T5 and DeBERTa backbones, CCHD and its variants consistently outperform MiniCheck, FactCG, and AlignScore on standard factuality benchmarks.

2 Method

Fig. 2 shows the key of CCHD framework: (i) a constrained training objective that enforces agreement across semantically equivalent paraphrase views (Sec. 2.1); and (ii) a Lagrangian optimization scheme to solve the constrained problem (Sec. 2.2). Finally, we introduce a practical instantiation of view generation via back-translation in Sec. 2.3.

2.1 Constrained Training Objective

Problem setup. Given a document dd and an LLM-generated claim cc, the task is to predict whether cc is supported or contradicted by dd. Let y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} be the ground-truth label and fθ​(d,c)∈[0,1]f_{\theta}(d,c)\in[0,1] the detector’s predicted probability that cc is consistent with dd. We denote predictions y^=fθ​(d,c)\hat{y}=f_{\theta}(d,c) for the original input, and y^p=fθ​(dp,cp)\hat{y}_{p}=f_{\theta}(d_{p},c_{p}) for paraphrased (dp,cp)(d_{p},c_{p}) via a paraphraser p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P} (e.g., back-translation [7]).

Primary objective. The primary goal is to minimize the cross-entropy on the original input:

ℒcls​(θ)=CE⁡(y,y^),\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathrm{CE}\big(y,\;\hat{y}\big), (1)

which encourages agreement between y^\hat{y} and yy.

Consistency constraints. Rather than simply appending paraphrased samples to the primary loss [7, 17], we (i) explicitly encode the semantic equivalence between original and paraphrased views, and (ii) accommodate potential noise in paraphrases. To this end, we impose prediction-level soft constraints for each view pp:

(C1)gp,1​(θ):=J⁡(y^,y^p)−ϵp,1≤ 0,\text{(C1)}\quad g_{p,1}(\theta)\;:=\;\mathrm{J}\big(\hat{y},\,\hat{y}_{p}\big)-\epsilon_{p,1}\;\leq\;0, (2)
(C2)gp,2​(θ):=CE⁡(y,y^p)−ϵp,2≤ 0,\text{(C2)}\quad g_{p,2}(\theta)\;:=\;\mathrm{CE}\big(y,\,\hat{y}_{p}\big)-\epsilon_{p,2}\;\leq\;0, (3)

where J(μ,ν)=12(KL(μ∥ν)+KL(ν∥μ))\mathrm{J}(\mu,\nu)=\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|\nu)+\mathrm{KL}(\nu\|\mu)\big) is the Jeffreys divergence [3], and ϵp,1,ϵp,2≥0\epsilon_{p,1},\epsilon_{p,2}\geq 0 are tolerances.

Constraint (2) encourages paraphrases consistency by bounding the divergence between prediction distributions before and after paraphrasing. Constraint (3) enforces label preservation for each paraphrase, with slack ϵp,2\epsilon_{p,2} to account for occasional paraphrase noise. C2 reinforces the assumption that paraphrase does not change the veracity of the claim.

All constraints are defined at the prediction level. However, an embedding-level variant (e.g., bounding distance between representations) is also possible without altering the framework, and is experimentally explored in Sec. 3.4.

2.2 Lagrangian Optimization via Gradient Descent–Ascent

Training under the constraints in Eqs. (2)-(3) is posed as a constrained optimization problem:

minθ⁡ℒcls​(θ)s.t.gp,i​(θ)≤0∀p∈𝒫,i∈{1,2}.\min_{\theta}\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\theta)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad g_{p,i}(\theta)\leq 0\;\;\;\;\forall\,p\!\in\!\mathcal{P},\;i\!\in\!\{1,2\}. (4)

To solve it, we form the Lagrangian by introducing nonnegative multipliers 𝝀={λp,i≥0|∀p,i}\boldsymbol{\lambda}=\{\lambda_{p,i}\geq 0\;|\;\forall p,i\}:

ℒ⁡(θ,𝝀)=ℒcls​(θ)+∑p∑iλp,i​gp,i​(θ).\mathcal{L}(\theta,\boldsymbol{\lambda})\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\theta)\;+\;\sum_{p}\sum_{i}\lambda_{p,i}\,g_{p,i}(\theta). (5)

It introduces only a handful of additional scalar variables (one per constraint), leaving the model architecture unchanged.

The goal is to find a saddle point (θ⋆,𝝀⋆)(\theta^{\star},\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\star}) that minimizes ℒ\mathcal{L} (Eq. (5)) in θ\theta and maximizes it in 𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda}. We adopt a primal-dual gradient descent-ascent (GDA) scheme [11]. In each training iteration, the updates of θ\theta and 𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda} are defined as:

θ\displaystyle\theta ←θ−η0​∇θℒ​(θ,𝝀),\displaystyle\leftarrow\theta-\eta_{0}\,\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta,\boldsymbol{\lambda}), (6)
λp,i\displaystyle\lambda_{p,i} ←[λp,i+ηp,i​gp,i​(θ)]+,\displaystyle\leftarrow\big[\lambda_{p,i}+\eta_{p,i}\,g_{p,i}(\theta)\big]_{+},

where η0,ηp,i>0\eta_{0},\eta_{p,i}>0 are learning rates for the primal and dual variables, respectively. [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+} denotes projection onto ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}. This subgradient ascent rule adaptively adjusts the penalty strength: λp,i\lambda_{p,i} will increase whenever the corresponding constraint is violated (e.g., J⁡(y^,y^p)>ϵp,1\mathrm{J}(\hat{y},\hat{y}_{p})>\epsilon_{p,1}), and decreases or leaves it unchanged when the constraint is satisfied.

2.3 Instantiation of CCHD

Choice of paraphrase. Among common paraphrasing strategies (e.g., perturb [1] and rewrite [18]), we adopt back-translation [7] for two practical reasons: (i) it induces broad stylistic and lexical variation while largely preserving semantics; and (ii) it can be implemented reliably and inexpensively with off-the-shelf machine translation (MT) systems [16], e.g., a commercial MT API11 1 https://translate.google.com, thereby avoiding LLM-based paraphrasers and additional annotation.

Extensions. CCHD naturally extends to multiple pivots and paraphrase strategies, at the cost of adding a few scalar dual multipliers λ\lambda only. Cross-view consistency can also be enforced via pairwise constraints, e.g., dpred​(y^p,y^q)−ϵp,q≤0d_{\text{pred}}(\hat{y}_{p},\hat{y}_{q})-\epsilon_{p,q}\leq 0 for two paraphrasers p≠qp\neq q, which plug into the same Lagrangian without altering the optimization procedure. In this paper, we adopt a single pivot to control cost and compare various pivots in Sec. 3.4.

Efficiency. CCHD is efficient during both training and inference. Training: it is label-efficient (no additional human annotation) and parameter-efficient (introducing only per-view dual scalars). Inference: paraphrase generation is performed offline for training only, so test-time cost matches that of the underlying Flan-T5/DeBERTa detector, preserving the runtime profile of standard discriminative baselines [17, 10].

3 Experiments

3.1 Experiment Settings

Model setup. We instantiate the detector with DeBERTa [6] (default) or Flan-T5 [5] without architectural changes, denoted with suffix -DBT and -FT5, respectively. A single pivot language (French by default) is used for back-translation to construct one paraphrase view per example. Analyses of backbone choice, pivot languages, and constraint design appear in Secs. 3.3 and 3.4.

Hyperparameters. The major settings follow FactCG [10]. The primal learning rate η0\eta_{0} is ×10−51\!\times\!10^{-5} for DeBERTa and ×10−55\!\times\!10^{-5} for Flan-T5. All dual variables use ηp,i=×10−3\eta_{p,i}=1\!\times\!10^{-3}. We set all tolerances ϵp,i=0\epsilon_{p,i}=0 and initialize the Lagrange multipliers 𝝀\boldsymbol{\lambda} from a uniform distribution.

Baselines. We compare against state-of-the-art non-LLM detectors: FactCC [7], SummaC [9], AlignScore [20], MiniCheck [17], and FactCG [10]. We use the authors’ released implementations and recommended checkpoints when available. Besides, we calibrate a decision threshold on the development split following each paper’s protocol.

Datasets and metrics. Evaluation follows the LLM-AggreFact benchmark, which aggregates 11 factuality/grounded-consistency datasets [17]. We adopt the official task definitions and splits, and report per-task F1 as well as macro-averaged F1 scores (AVG).

3.2 Main Results

Table 1 reports F1 (%) across the 11 tasks in LLM-AggreFact. CCHD-DBT and CCHD-FT5 achieve the strongest average performance, with macro-F1 of 79.73 and 79.11, respectively. CCHD-DBT exceeds the best non-CCHD baseline (FactCG-FT5, 78.47) by +1.26 points while retaining the efficiency of discriminative detectors (with ∼\sim50% fewer parameters). Regarding per-task performance, CCHD is the winner on the majority of tasks (7/11), indicating robustness and generalization across tasks.

Across backbones. Both DeBERTa and Flan-T5 instantiations of CCHD outperform their backbone-matched baselines, suggesting that the gains arise from the constrained objective with GDA rather than backbone-specific factors.

Summary. Optimizing paraphrase-consistency and label-preserving constraints via GDA yields consistent, cross-dataset improvements without inference-time overhead, establishing CCHD as a superior discriminative detector.

3.3 Ablation Study

To disentangle the effects of the GDA scheme and the two constraint families in Eqs. (2) and (3), we evaluate: C1 only (paraphrase-consistency, Eq. (2)), C2 only (label-preservation, Eq. 3), and Fixed λ\lambda (include both constraints with fixed λ\lambda; no GDA).

Overall effect of GDA and joint constraints. As visualized in Fig. 3, the per-task F1 distribution of CCHD is noticeably right-shifted relative to all ablated variants. Macro-averaged over 11 tasks, CCHD attains the highest F1 of 79.73, exceeding C1 only (78.43; +1.30 pp), C2 only (77.38; +2.36 pp), and Fixed λ\lambda (77.29; +2.44 pp).

Effect of each constraint. C1 only leverages paraphrase-consistency and attains the second-best macro-F1, but can drift under noisy paraphrases without an explicit label tether. C2 only anchors paraphrases to ground-truth labels, yet is sensitive to augmentation noise and less invariant to paraphrastic variation. CCHD jointly enforces both constraints with adaptive multipliers, and strikes the best accuracy across tasks.

3.4 Sensitivity Analysis

Setup. Using the DeBERTa backbone, we vary (i) the pivot language for back-translation: French (fr), Chinese (zh), Spanish (es); and (ii) the paraphrase-consistency design: a prediction-level constraint (“pred”, Eq. (2)) that penalizes divergence between output distributions, and an embedding-level constraint (“embd”) that penalizes the ℓ1\ell_{1} distance between [CLS] representations. Results appear in Table 2.

Comparison to baselines. Across the six CCHD variants, macro-F1 ranges from 78.03 to 79.73. Every variant significantly exceeds all DeBERTa-based baselines in Table 1 (FactCC, AlignScore, MiniCheck-DBT, FactCG-DBT).

Effect of pivot language. All three pivots are competitive, but French yields the strongest averages under both designs: fr-pred and fr-embd achieves the best overall macro-F1 comparing to zh and es counterparts. However, task-level performance is complementary: zh-pred attains the top scores on AggreFact-CNN and TofuEval-MeetB; while es-pred leads on REVEAL and LFQA. It could because fr↔\leftrightarrowen MT systems are historically strong and syntactically closer than zh↔\leftrightarrowen and es↔\leftrightarrowen. It may yield paraphrases that better preserve semantics while still varying surface form (less semantic drift), thus providing a cleaner consistency signal.

Effect of constraint design. Prediction-level consistency outperforms embedding-level consistency for each pivot. While embd can be favorable on structure-sensitive tasks (e.g., WiCE, Claim Verify), pred dominates on most others and yields more stable gains overall. The potential reason could be aligning predictions directly regularizes the decision boundary and complements the primary cross-entropy, whereas embedding-level constraints are sensitive to representation scaling and may under- or over-constrain learning.

4 Conclusion

We presented the Consistency-Constrained Hallucination Detector, which enfores paraphrase consistency and label-preservation constraints. Instantiated via back-translation, CCHD delivers significant F1 gains across 11 factuality datasets without extra inference time. To further enhance the generalization and reliability of CCHD, we will explore: (i) combining multiple pivot languages and non-MT paraphrasers with adaptive selection; and (ii) extending evaluation to hallucinations produced by multimodal LLMs [2].
